items.prompt: Why is an editor's undo button instant?
choices: It kept the previous state ready to put back
It recomputes the document from the first draft
It asks a server to rebuild the file
items.explanation: The previous version already exists, so undo only has to put it back. Rebuilding from scratch is the slow alternative.

items.prompt: What is a deployable artifact?
choices: The source code the team edits and reviews
The ticket that tracks the change request
The built, ready-to-run output of a deploy
items.explanation: An artifact is the compiled or packaged result, such as a container image, as opposed to the source it came from.

items.prompt: A team rolls back by rebuilding the old version from source. Where does the extra time go?
choices: Waiting for every user to log out first
Building and testing it again first
Deleting the bad version's old logs
items.explanation: The rebuild path adds build, test and redeploy steps that a kept artifact skips.

items.prompt: Which rollback is faster?
choices: Redeploying an artifact kept from before
Rebuilding from the source repository
Writing and testing a brand-new fix
items.explanation: A kept artifact needs no build step, only a deploy aimed at the older tag.

items.prompt: When is the best time to decide how rollbacks will work?
choices: During the 2am incident itself
Only after the post-mortem is written
Well before any incident happens
items.explanation: Deciding during an incident is when it is most likely to be decided badly, so the mechanics are planned in advance.

items.prompt: Turning a feature flag off is a rollback that needs what?
choices: A full rebuild of the app
No redeploy needed at all
A database migration
items.explanation: The old behavior is still in the code, so switching the flag restores it without shipping anything.

items.prompt: What does a blue-green setup keep ready?
choices: The previous environment, kept warm
Only a copy of the source code
A backup of the team's issue tracker
items.explanation: Rolling back is switching traffic to the environment that was already running the old version.

items.prompt: A registry deletes each old image once a deploy succeeds. What happens at the next rollback?
choices: It is faster, because there is less to search
Nothing changes, since git has the code
It has to rebuild the old version first
items.explanation: With the artifact gone, the old version must be rebuilt from source, which is the slow path.

items.prompt: A rebuild-from-source rollback takes 40 minutes and a kept-artifact rollback takes 2 minutes. At 150 failed requests per minute, how many more requests fail on the slower path?
choices: 6,000 requests (the whole slow path)
5,700 requests (38 extra minutes)
300 requests (the whole fast path)
11,400 requests (double the gap)
items.explanation: The gap is 40 - 2 = 38 minutes, and 38 x 150 = 5,700. The other numbers are totals for one path or a doubling.
items.reference:
Fast rollback is decided before the incident
kept artifact: redeploy in minutes
source only: build and test first, then deploy
keep it under an immutable version tag
Why: speed comes from preparation, not from a faster decision.
items.learnMore:
Ready artifacts

A rollback is fast when the previous version already exists as something that can run. Keeping each deploy's artifact for a retention window turns a rollback into the ordinary deploy mechanism aimed at an older tag.

Common mistake

Believing that having the code in version control means a rollback is instant. Source still has to be built and tested before it can serve traffic.
items.reflection: Think of something you can restore quickly only because a copy was kept. What would restoring it cost if the copy had never been made?

items.prompt: A team says every commit lives in git forever, so they can roll back instantly. What is wrong with that?
choices: Source history is not a running version, it still needs building
Old commits are deleted whenever a branch is removed from the repository
Rebuilt commits behave differently on every single build run
Only the newest commit is ever allowed to run in production
items.explanation: Version control keeps the recipe, not the cooked result. Speed needs a ready-to-run artifact.

items.prompt: A pipeline tags every image `latest`, overwriting the previous one. Why does that hurt rollbacks?
choices: The latest tag cannot run on more than one server at once
Tags are only read by the build step and never by the deploy
Overwriting a tag stops the new version from starting up
Old images stay but the tag no longer points to them
items.explanation: A rollback targets an older tag. If that tag was overwritten, the old artifact cannot be addressed even if bytes remain.

items.prompt: Which retention policy best supports fast rollback?
choices: Only the running version, to avoid any confusion in the deploy tool
One artifact per month, chosen to match the planned release calendar and nothing else
Several recent versions, kept past the usual time to notice a bad deploy
Each artifact only until the next deploy's own tests have passed
items.explanation: Retention has to cover the window in which a rollback might still be wanted, not the next test run.

items.prompt: What is a roll-forward?
choices: Redeploying the previous version again
Shipping a new fix on top of the bad version
Pausing every deploy for a full week
items.explanation: Roll-forward means moving ahead with a corrected version instead of returning to the old one.

items.prompt: What is a rollback?
choices: Returning to the previous known-good version
Shipping a fix on top of the bad version
Deleting the bad commit from history
items.explanation: A rollback puts back a version that was already working.

items.prompt: The cause is unknown, and the old version is ready and compatible. Which move?
choices: Roll forward with a guessed fix
Leave it running and keep watching
Roll back, then diagnose
items.explanation: Restoring a known-good state first is safer than gambling on a guess during an incident.

items.prompt: Why is rollback the usual default?
choices: It never needs to touch the database or schema
It restores a state already known to work
It is always cheaper than writing a fix
items.explanation: The old version has already proven itself in production, which an untested fix has not.

items.prompt: A migration already dropped a column the old code needs. Which move?
choices: Roll forward
Roll back anyway
Do nothing at all
items.explanation: Redeploying the old code would crash against the changed schema, so the way out is a fix going forward.

items.prompt: Which is a good reason to roll forward?
choices: The team likes writing new code more
The incident started during a weekend
Going back would crash on current data
items.explanation: The only good reason is that the rollback itself would be unsafe.

items.prompt: In a rollback, when does diagnosis happen?
choices: Before any action is taken at all
Once service has been restored
Only if the bug comes back
items.explanation: Rollback stops the damage first, which gives the team calm time to find the cause.

items.prompt: A well-understood one-line bug has a tested fix ready. What is reasonable?
choices: Either one, by weighing the risk of each
Only ever rolling back, never forward
Waiting for a quiet hour to decide
items.explanation: When the cause is known and the fix is tested, both options can be sound, so the lower-risk one wins.

items.prompt: v42 wrote orders in a new format that v41 cannot read, then started failing. v41's artifact is ready. What is the better move?
choices: Roll back, since the old version is always the safest state to return to
Roll forward, since redeploying v41 would leave the new orders unreadable
Roll back, since a ready artifact always means that a rollback is safe to run
Roll forward, since a fix is always faster to ship than any redeploy
items.explanation: Readiness of the artifact is not the same as compatibility with the data already written. Here going back is the unsafe direction.
items.reference:
Default to rollback, unless going back is unsafe
old version ready and compatible: roll back
data already changed in a way old code cannot read: roll forward
cause unknown: roll back now, diagnose after
Why: rollback returns to a state known to work, so it is the default.
items.learnMore:
Rolling back or rolling forward

A rollback restores the previous version. A roll-forward ships a new fix on top of the bad one. Restoring service with a known-good state is usually safer than writing an untested fix under pressure, unless the data has moved in a way the old code cannot handle.

Common mistake

Rolling back by reflex after new-format data has been written, which can leave records the old code cannot read.
items.reflection: Think of a project where going back would have cost more than pushing on. What made going back unsafe?

items.prompt: The cause is unknown, v41 is ready, and the schema is unchanged. On-call proposes guessing a fix. What is the objection?
choices: It adds an untested change mid-incident, where rollback restores a known state
Fixes can never pass through the pipeline while an incident is open
A guessed fix is only wrong when the bug turns out to be inside the database layer
Rolling forward is unsafe whenever an old artifact is still available
items.explanation: The objection is about risk, not process: an untested change under pressure can add a second failure.

Should v41 also be rebuilt from source?
Did data or a dependency cause the errors instead?
Can the rollback simply be repeated until it works?
items.explanation: If the old code still fails, the cause lies outside the code change, so the diagnosis should widen to data and dependencies.

items.prompt: What does expand-contract do first?
choices: Drops the old column straight away
Renames the column in place at once
Adds the new column and removes nothing
items.explanation: Expand means adding the new structure while keeping the old one, so both code versions still work.

items.prompt: When is the old column dropped?
choices: In the very same deploy as the code change
In a later deploy, after the rollback window
Never, since a column can never be dropped at all
items.explanation: The drop waits until the rollback window has passed, so no old code needs the column.

items.prompt: Why can redeploying old code fail after a bad deploy?
choices: The schema may have changed under it
Old code is always slower
Artifacts expire after one hour on disk
items.explanation: The code is restored but the database is not, so the two can disagree.

items.prompt: Is adding a nullable column that the old code ignores rollback-safe?
choices: No, any added column always breaks old code
Only if the table happens to be empty
Yes, since the old code never touches it
items.explanation: Code that never references a column is unaffected by it.

items.prompt: Is renaming a column in place rollback-safe?
choices: Yes, because names are only labels
No, one code version looks for the wrong name
Yes, if the change is done overnight
items.explanation: The old code wants the old name and the new code wants the new one, so a rollback breaks whichever does not match.

items.prompt: During the expand phase, the new code writes what?
choices: Both the old and the new column
Only the new column
Only the old column
items.explanation: Writing both keeps either version's reads correct.

items.prompt: What does backward-compatible migration mean?
choices: It can be undone by restoring from a backup
It only ever runs on older databases
Old and new code can both run against it
items.explanation: Compatibility is about code versions working against the same schema, not about restoring backups.

items.prompt: Drop a column the old code reads, then roll back. What happens?
choices: The rollback finishes much faster
The old code crashes on reading it
The column comes back by itself
items.explanation: Redeploying code does not restore a dropped column.

items.prompt: Which migration is safe to ship in a deploy that might be rolled back?
choices: Renaming a column that the old code is still reading
Adding a nullable column that the old code never references
Dropping a column that the old code is still reading on every request
Changing a column to a type the old code cannot parse
items.explanation: Only an addition the old code ignores leaves both versions working. The others each break the old code.
items.reference:
Both code versions must fit the schema
drop or rename a column the old code reads: rollback breaks
add a nullable column the old code ignores: safe
expand now (write both), contract later: safe
Why: a rollback is only safe while the old code still works against today's schema.
items.learnMore:
The migration trap and expand-contract

Application code and the database are deployed separately but must agree at every moment, including right after a rollback. Expand-contract adds the new structure first and writes both, then removes the old structure in a later deploy once the rollback window has passed.

Common mistake

Dropping or renaming a column in the same deploy as the code change, which leaves the old code with nothing to read.
items.reflection: Think of two things that must change together but cannot change at the same instant, such as a form and its spreadsheet. How would you order the changes so that stopping halfway never breaks either?

items.prompt: What is the safe sequence for replacing column A with column B?
choices: Add B, write both columns, drop A later
Drop A, add B, then write only to B
Rename A to B, then deploy the new code afterwards
Add B, drop A at once, then start writing to B
items.explanation: Every step keeps a column the old code needs until no old code remains.

The health check reverted the wrong version
The code was restored, but not the column it reads
items.explanation: Code and schema are rolled back separately. The old code is fine, but its column is gone.

items.prompt: When is it safe to run the contract step that drops the old column?
choices: Right after the new code starts serving traffic
In the same transaction as the expand step
Once the rollback window passes with no revert
Before the new code is deployed at all
items.explanation: Dropping earlier removes the very column a rollback would need.

items.prompt: What is flapping?
choices: A trigger so jumpy it flags healthy deploys
A rollback that takes too long to finish
A deploy that alternates between two servers
items.explanation: Flapping means too many false rollbacks, which erodes trust in the automation.

items.prompt: Why wait for several bad windows before rolling back?
choices: To give users time to log out first
Because artifacts need time to warm up
To tell a lasting problem from noise
items.explanation: One bad window may be a blip, while several in a row is a pattern.

items.prompt: What happens if too many bad windows are required?
choices: Too many false rollbacks start to happen
Reaction is slow while failures continue
The kept artifact gets much larger
items.explanation: Each extra window is another minute of failing traffic.

items.prompt: A window of 4 requests shows 1 error (25%). What does the check do first?
choices: Sets it aside as too little data to judge
Rolls back at once, treating it as a severe window
Marks the deploy healthy right away
items.explanation: A rate from a handful of requests is not trustworthy, so the sample size is checked first.

items.prompt: Which signal can skip the confirmation windows?
choices: A mild one-time latency uptick
A single failed request
A severe error spike, like 40%
items.explanation: Noise does not plausibly produce a spike that large, so waiting adds no confidence.

items.prompt: Which signal should go to a person?
choices: A sharp, sustained spike of 500 errors
An ambiguous, borderline signal
A 40% error rate
items.explanation: Ambiguous signals need context a threshold cannot hold.

items.prompt: What resets the bad-window count?
choices: A good window
A bad window
A slow rollback
items.explanation: Bad windows must be consecutive, so a good one starts the count over.

items.prompt: What does a health check watch after a deploy?
choices: Only the number of commits
Only the build time
Error rate and latency
items.explanation: Health checks watch behavior in production, such as errors and response time.

items.prompt: At 150 failed requests per minute with one-minute windows, how many requests fail before a 10-bad-window trigger even acts?
choices: 450 requests (3 minutes)
1,500 requests (10 minutes)
150 requests (1 minute)
6,000 requests (40 minutes)
items.explanation: Ten windows of one minute each is 10 minutes, and 10 x 150 = 1,500.
items.reference:
Confirmation trades false rollbacks for reaction time
1 window: reacts fast, flaps on noise
3 windows: filters a blip, about 3 minutes of delay
10 windows: very sure, about 10 minutes of delay
severe spike: act at once
Why: more confirmation means fewer false rollbacks but a slower reaction, and a very clear signal needs none.
items.learnMore:
Tuning an automatic trigger

The check watches windows of traffic. Requiring several bad windows in a row filters noise, but every extra window is a minute of failing traffic. A severe spike is clear enough to skip confirmation, and ambiguous signals are better handed to a person.

Common mistake

Treating the window count as a constant to set once. It depends on how noisy the system's normal metrics are.
items.reflection: Think of an alert, such as a smoke detector or a bank fraud text, that you learned to ignore. Was it too jumpy, and what would you change about it?

items.prompt: A team sets the trigger to 1 bad window. What is the most likely result within weeks?
choices: Noise rolls back healthy deploys and people disable it
Real regressions are caught more slowly than they were before the change
Rollbacks stop needing a kept artifact to work
Severe spikes are no longer detected by the check
items.explanation: One window offers no protection against noise, which causes flapping and a loss of trust.

items.prompt: Errors per 100 requests across four windows are 6, 1, 2, 1, and three bad windows are needed to roll back. What happens?
choices: Rollback at window 1, because 6% is above the 5% threshold
Rollback at window 4, because four windows were seen in total
No decision yet, because nothing resets a bad window count
No rollback: the lone bad window resets and three good ones follow
items.explanation: A good window resets the bad count, so the single blip never reaches three, and three good windows follow.

items.prompt: Why does a 40% error rate skip the three-window rule?
choices: Severe windows are always counted as three bad windows
The rule only ever applies to latency and not to error rates

A person must approve it, so the automatic rule is skipped

items.prompt: Implement `errorRate(errors, sample)`: the share of requests that failed, as a fraction.
items.explanation: The error rate is the failed requests divided by all requests in the window.

items.prompt: Implement `isBad(rate, threshold)`: true when the rate is at or above the threshold.
items.explanation: The threshold itself counts as bad, so the comparison is greater-or-equal.

items.prompt: Implement `hasEnoughData(sample, min)`: true when the window has at least `min` requests.
items.explanation: A window with exactly the minimum is enough, so the comparison is greater-or-equal.

items.prompt: Implement `failedRequests(rpm, ratePercent, minutes)`: how many requests fail in total, rounded to a whole number.
items.explanation: Total requests are rpm times minutes, and the failing share is the percentage divided by 100.

items.prompt: Implement `nextBadCount(count, windowIsBad)`: one more bad window in a row if this one is bad, otherwise back to zero.
items.explanation: Bad windows must be consecutive, so any good window resets the count.

items.prompt: Implement `isSevere(errors, sample, severeRate)`: true when the window's error rate is at or above `severeRate`.
items.explanation: Compute the rate, then compare with greater-or-equal so the boundary counts as severe.

items.prompt: Implement `allBad(statuses)`: true when the list is not empty and every status is `"bad"`.
items.explanation: An empty list has no bad windows at all, so it must not count as all bad.

items.prompt: Implement `lastStatus(statuses)`: the most recent status, or `"none"` if the list is empty.
items.explanation: The newest window is the last element, and an empty list needs its own answer.

items.prompt: Implement `classifyWindow(errors, sample)`. Return `"insufficient-data"` if `sample` is under 50. Otherwise compute the error rate and return `"severe"` at 0.25 or more, `"bad"` at 0.05 or more, else `"good"`.
items.explanation: The sample size is checked first because a rate from few requests means nothing. Then the larger threshold is tested before the smaller, or severe windows would be reported as merely bad.
items.reference:
The decision is a small state machine
each window: classify it (insufficient, good, bad, severe)
good resets the bad count; bad resets the good count
too little data leaves both counts unchanged
Why: once each rule is named, each is a line or two of code.

Writing the rollback decision

Classify each window, then update two counters from the verdict, then decide from the counters. Keeping each step a small pure function makes every rule easy to test on its own.

Common mistake

Forgetting that a window with too little data should change nothing, or that a good window must reset the bad count.
items.reflection: Think of a rule you apply only if something happens N times in a row, like a streak counter. What resets it, and what leaves it unchanged?

items.prompt: Implement `shouldRollback(statuses)`. `statuses` lists window verdicts in order (`"good"`, `"bad"`, `"severe"`, `"insufficient-data"`). Return true if the latest is `"severe"`, or if the last three are all `"bad"`.
items.explanation: A severe latest window triggers at once. Otherwise the last three must all be bad, and fewer than three windows cannot qualify, so a short list is rejected.
items.reference:
The decision is a small state machine
each window: classify it (insufficient, good, bad, severe)
good resets the bad count; bad resets the good count
too little data leaves both counts unchanged
Why: once each rule is named, each is a line or two of code.

items.prompt: Implement `rollbackMinute(statuses, needed)`. `statuses` holds one `"good"` or `"bad"` per minute. Return the 1-based minute at which `needed` bad windows in a row is first reached, or -1 if it never is. A good window restarts the count.
items.explanation: A running count goes up on bad windows and resets on good ones. The first minute where it reaches the needed length is the answer, shifted by one because minutes are 1-based.

items.prompt: Implement `updateCounters(state, status)`. `state` is `{ bad, good }`. A `"bad"` status gives `{ bad: bad + 1, good: 0 }`. A `"good"` status gives `{ bad: 0, good: good + 1 }`. Any other status (such as `"insufficient-data"`) returns the counts unchanged. Keep the key order `bad`, then `good`.
items.explanation: Each verdict advances its own counter and clears the other. A window with too little data says nothing about the deploy, so it leaves both counts as they were.
